cls: Parenteral nutrition - crystalline amino acid (protein/nitrogen source) injection
pharm: Sterile mixture of essential and nonessential L-amino acids providing a nitrogen source for protein synthesis in parenteral (total or partial) nutrition.
quick: Individualized: typically ~1-2 g amino acid/kg/day IV, titrated to protein needs and tolerance
Intravenous nutrition; given when enteral route is unavailable or inadequate
Use if clearly needed for nutritional support; no specific contraindication beyond underlying disease
May be used when nutritionally indicated
Reduce/individualize in renal impairment; monitor BUN, electrolytes, acid-base
Contraindicated in hepatic coma; use cautiously and monitor ammonia/LFTs
Electrolytes, glucose, BUN, ammonia, acid-base, fluid balance, LFTs
summary: Amino acid injection is a sterile solution of essential and nonessential L-amino acids used as the nitrogen (protein) source in parenteral nutrition for patients in whom oral or enteral feeding is impossible, inadequate, or contraindicated, or whose protein needs are increased (e.g., burns, hypercatabolism). It is given intravenously via central or peripheral routes, must be diluted with dextrose (and combined with lipid, electrolytes, vitamins, and trace elements) to provide complete nutrition, and the dose is fully individualized to protein requirements and metabolic tolerance. It is contraindicated in untreated anuria, hepatic coma, inborn errors of amino acid metabolism, and hypersensitivity to any component. Close metabolic monitoring (electrolytes, glucose, BUN, ammonia, acid-base) is essential.
indications: Nutritional support (total or partial parenteral nutrition) to prevent or treat negative nitrogen balance when the alimentary tract cannot or should not be used
Patients in whom gastrointestinal absorption of protein is impaired
Patients with substantially increased protein requirements (e.g., extensive burns, hypercatabolic states)
Nutritional support of infants (including low birth weight) and young children requiring TPN (pediatric formulations)

dosage.d: Individualized to protein needs, commonly ~1-2 g amino acid/kg/day; advance gradually with adequate nonprotein calories
dosage.n: Dilute with dextrose; add lipid, electrolytes, vitamins, trace elements

dosage.d: Up to 2.5 g amino acid/kg/day; start ~1 g/kg/day and increase by ~0.5 g/kg/day to target
Up to 25 g/day for the first 10 kg, plus 1-1.25 g/kg/day for each kg over 10 kg
dosage.n: Constrain by relatively higher pediatric fluid and caloric needs

admin: Administer intravenously by central venous infusion (when admixed with hypertonic dextrose) or peripheral vein (lower osmolarity solutions only)
Dilute/admix with dextrose and provide nonprotein calories; do not infuse hypertonic central-line solutions peripherally
Use aseptic compounding (laminar flow) and an in-line filter; do not add medications unless compatibility is established
Initiate slowly and advance gradually to allow metabolic adaptation; provide concurrent lipid, electrolytes, vitamins, and trace elements
Inspect for particulate matter, precipitate, or discoloration before use; discard unused admixed solution per institutional limits
moa: Amino acid injections supply a balanced mixture of essential and nonessential L-amino acids that serve as substrate for protein synthesis. When infused together with nonprotein calories (dextrose and/or lipid), the amino acids are utilized for anabolism rather than as an energy source, restoring positive nitrogen balance, supporting tissue repair and immune function, and preventing the catabolism of endogenous protein. Pediatric formulations are designed to produce plasma amino acid profiles approximating those of a normally fed infant.

absolute: Inborn errors of amino acid metabolism (e.g., maple syrup urine disease, isovaleric acidemia)
Hypersensitivity to one or more amino acids present in the solution
Severe uncorrected electrolyte or acid-base disturbances and fluid overload states (until corrected)
relative: Renal impairment/azotemia (use specialized formulas, reduce nitrogen load)
Hepatic impairment (monitor ammonia; use as indicated)
monitor: Serum electrolytes, glucose, and acid-base balance
Liver function tests and serum proteins

preg: There are no adequate controlled studies; amino acid solutions are used during pregnancy when parenteral nutritional support is clinically required. Use guided by maternal nutritional need and standard parenteral nutrition monitoring.
lact: Amino acid parenteral nutrition may be used in breastfeeding women when nutritionally indicated; it provides physiologic nutrients and is not expected to harm the breastfed infant.
renal: In renal impairment, the nitrogen load and fluid/electrolyte content must be reduced or a specialized (essential amino acid) formula used; monitor BUN, creatinine, electrolytes, and acid-base status closely.
hepatic: Contraindicated in hepatic coma. In other hepatic impairment, use cautiously with monitoring of blood ammonia and liver function; specialized branched-chain-enriched formulas may be used in encephalopathy.

major: Incompatible additives causing precipitation (e.g., calcium-phosphate precipitation, certain medications) - can cause fatal particulate embolism if infused
moderate: Insulin requirements change with concurrent dextrose - monitor and adjust glucose control
Drugs added to the admixture must be confirmed compatible (e.g., some antibiotics, electrolytes)
minor: Tetracyclines may reduce the protein-sparing effect of parenteral amino acids
interactions.food: Used in place of, or to supplement, enteral feeding when the GI tract cannot be used.
interactions.diagnostics: Can alter blood glucose, BUN, ammonia, electrolytes, and liver enzymes; interpret laboratory monitoring in the context of nutrition support.

common: Hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia (related to dextrose component)
serious: Hepatobiliary dysfunction / cholestasis with prolonged TPN
rare: Hypersensitivity reactions to amino acids or additives
Aluminum toxicity with prolonged use in renal impairment/neonates
emergency: Severe metabolic derangement (acidosis, hyperammonemia, severe electrolyte shifts)

monitoring: Serum electrolytes, glucose, BUN/creatinine, and acid-base balance regularly (more frequently at initiation)
Blood ammonia, especially in infants and hepatic impairment
Liver function tests and serum proteins periodically
Fluid balance, daily weight, and signs of fluid overload
Catheter site for infection and signs of refeeding syndrome (phosphate, potassium, magnesium)
counsel: This is intravenous nutrition given when you cannot eat or absorb enough food
Report fever, chills, or redness/pain at the IV/catheter site - signs of catheter infection
Blood tests will be done regularly to balance your salts, sugar, and protein
Tell your team about excessive thirst, swelling, breathlessness, or confusion
Do not let any other medicine be added to the bag unless the pharmacist has confirmed it is compatible
pk: Amino acids enter the metabolic pool immediately upon infusion
Plasma amino acid levels reflect infusion rate; steady state during continuous infusion
Individual amino acids are rapidly utilized/turned over (minutes to hours)
Anabolic effect persists during continuous administration with adequate calories
Store at room temperature, protected from freezing and excessive heat; admixtures per compounding limits
pearls: Provides the nitrogen (protein) source of parenteral nutrition - must be combined with dextrose, lipid, electrolytes, vitamins, and trace elements for complete TPN
Hypertonic (central) TPN requires a central line; only low-osmolarity solutions may be given peripherally
Contraindicated in untreated anuria, hepatic coma, inborn errors of amino acid metabolism, and component hypersensitivity
Advance slowly and watch for refeeding syndrome (phosphate, potassium, magnesium) in malnourished patients
Pediatric/neonatal formulas (with added cysteine/taurine) are specially designed to mimic a normally fed infant's plasma amino acid profile
missed: Amino acid parenteral nutrition is administered as a continuous or cyclic infusion managed by the clinical team rather than as discrete patient-taken doses; interruptions or rate changes should be managed by the care team to avoid metabolic swings (e.g., rebound hypoglycemia after abrupt cessation).
overdose: Excessive infusion (or too-rapid administration) can cause hyperammonemia, metabolic acidosis, azotemia, electrolyte disturbances, and fluid overload. Management is to stop or reduce the infusion and correct the metabolic and fluid/electrolyte abnormalities with supportive care; treat hyperammonemia and acidosis specifically. Reassess the prescription and infusion rate before resuming.
